ISL-ViT-Tiny

A compact factorised Vision Transformer for Indian Sign Language recognition, evaluated under a session-disjoint protocol that removes the leakage hidden in the standard benchmark.

Two things a panel will test — stated up front

The headline is one model at 2.0 MB, quoted as a three-seed mean. 85.9 % top-1 (INT4, quantisation-aware; seeds 84.5 / 87.5 / 85.8). No epoch or seed was chosen by test score, and it is measured on a test set re-extracted exactly as the live app extracts video. The gain over the pixel-only model (mean 73.7 %) comes from feeding the hand landmarks MediaPipe was already computing; paired on identical clips, p < 1e-8 for all three seeds.

Results vary by seed, so means are quoted. The pixel-only model spans 75.0 / 73.7 / 72.2 % across three seeds; the landmark model 87.3 / 86.9 / 85.4 %. A fine-tuning trick that looked like +2.8 on one seed moved two others in opposite directions and was rejected.

01

Problem Statement, Introduction & Motivation

4 marks

Application domain

Vision-based isolated sign language recognition (ISLR) — classifying a short video containing one sign into a word. This is the classification building block of a continuous recognition and translation system. The target deployment is a wearable assistant (smart glasses) that reads a sign and renders it as text or speech for a hearing listener.

The exact problem

Indian Sign Language is the primary language of roughly 63 million people with hearing impairment in India, and almost no hearing person understands it. Automatic ISL recognition must therefore run on a wearable device, on ordinary video, and be accurate enough on signers it has never seen to be relied on. Existing benchmarks do not test that last condition.

Why it is hard

  • Two hands plus the face. ISL is largely two-handed, and meaning depends on handshape, motion and location — the same handshape at forehead and at chest are different words.
  • Very little labelled data. INCLUDE provides ~16 clips per word; the 50-word benchmark trains on 571 clips total, about 11 per class. Vision transformers are normally trained on three orders of magnitude more.
  • A hard compute budget. Smart glasses cannot run a 300 M-parameter video model. The target is a few megabytes of weights and a few milliseconds per clip.

The existing limitation this project addresses

Published ISL systems report 94–99 % accuracy. Those numbers are produced on random splits, in which clips of the same signer, recorded in the same session, appear in both the training and the test set. Such a number does not predict performance on a new signer, which is the only situation a deployed product is ever in.

Evaluation protocolWhat can leak into the test setTop-1Gap vs control
random-videoNear-duplicate takes and shared recording sessions98.5 %—
take-groupShared recording sessions only44.1 %−54.4
session-disjointnothing75.6 %−22.9

Motivation

Twenty-three of those points are leakage. The contribution of this project is to measure ISL recognition honestly and then raise the honest number — from 42.1 % to 85.9 % on the same unchanged test set, in a single model that fits in 2.0 MB — rather than to add another leaky benchmark result.

Why a tiny factorised ViT is the appropriate approach

Transformers model long-range spatial and temporal structure, which sign language requires. But with ~11 training clips per class, a full-frame video transformer has ample capacity to memorise the room and the signer instead of the sign. Cropping the input to three anatomical streams removes background and signer appearance entirely, and factorising attention over space and then time reduces the attention cost by roughly 48× (derivation in §6). That combination is what makes a 3.76 M-parameter model viable on this much data and this little compute.

How the literature leads to this architecture

Architecture choice

SignViT and Shawon et al. establish that attention discriminates visually similar gestures and that ViViT-family models beat CNN baselines on word-level SLR. Abdi & Barzegar Touchahi show attention degrades more gracefully than convolution under corrupted input. → a video ViT is the right family.

Size choice

TinyMSLR shows distillation moves a transformer toward edge inference at 2.7 M parameters; Venkatappa et al. reach a 1,097 KB model at 16.2 ms on a smartphone — but on landmarks, not RGB. → a few-megabyte RGB model is the open question, and its size must be a measured file.

Evaluation choice

Alyami, Chalotonpised and López-Nava all treat signer-independent partitions as standard; Arib et al. name signer and background discrepancy as the limiting factor. → session/signer-disjoint evaluation is mandatory, and 75–80 % is the honest regime.

The gap this project occupies. Venkatappa et al. reach ~1 MB and 16 ms — on landmark sequences, which discard the fine-grained appearance an RGB frame carries. Ashfaq et al. show a ViT discriminates visually similar gestures — without any size constraint. TinyMSLR shows distillation works — at 2.7 M parameters on a 20-class benchmark. No surveyed work combines an RGB Vision Transformer, a few-megabyte budget, Indian Sign Language, and a signer-disjoint protocol. That intersection is what ISL-ViT-Tiny occupies.
Honest discrepancies between the case-study targets and what has been measured

The supplied EdgeSign-ViT case study specifies 224×224 input, 1–2 MB, 25–30 FPS, <30 ms/frame, <50 MB RAM on ARM devices. What this project has actually measured differs and should not be presented as if it met those targets:

  • Input is 64×64 per crop, not 224×224 — three anatomical crops per frame rather than a full frame. 96 px was tested and lost (−1.5, −0.9 points).
  • The 2.0 MB model is INT4 with quantisation-aware training. The file size is measured on the packed state dict; the INT4 kernels themselves have not yet been benchmarked on target hardware.
  • Latency is ~24 ms per clip on a desktop CPU, not per frame and not on ARM. No Raspberry Pi, smartphone or smart-glasses measurement exists yet.
  • Knowledge distillation, structured pruning and token pruning are not yet applied. A distillation harness exists and is verified but untrained.

Overall Application Architecture

5 marks

Tensor shape at every stage

StageShapeNote
Raw clip(F, H, W, 3)F ≈ 50–120 frames
Sample + letterbox(32, 720, 1280, 3)fixed working resolution for MediaPipe
Detect + crop → cache(32, 3, 128, 128, 3)uint8 memmap; L hand / R hand / face
Train-time sample(16, 3, 64, 64, 3)16 of 32 = 2× jitter headroom
Patch embed(48, 17, 192)48 crops × (16 patches + [cls])
Stage A output(16, 3, 192)class token per crop
Stream fusion(16, 192)3d → d, plus time embedding
Stage B → pool(192,)mean over 16 timesteps
Head(50,)logits → softmax

What the model actually sees

Two honest observations from Figure 3.2. “quiet” is a one-handed sign, so its left-hand stream is nearly static across all six timesteps and carries little information for that word. And the crop boxes overlap — at t = 12 in “loud” the left-hand crop also contains the face. The streams are anatomically named, not anatomically disjoint; this is a property of margin-based cropping.
Training and inference share one preprocessing path. predict.py calls the same extract_clip() and prepare_clip() functions that built the training cache — a separate inference preprocessor is the standard way a model that scores well offline fails on real video.

Deep Learning Architecture — ISL-ViT-Tiny

5 marks

a. Diagram · b. Explanation · c. Novelty proposed · d. Time and space complexity.

a · Architecture diagram

b · Component explanation

ComponentDetail
Input16 timesteps × 3 crops × 64×64×3, plus a per-crop box geometry vector and a binary detected flag. The model never receives a full video frame.
Patch / token creationEach 64×64 crop is split into 16 non-overlapping 16×16 patches. 48 crops × 16 patches = 768 patch tokens per clip.
EmbeddingLinear projection E ∈ ℝ768×192 maps each flattened patch to d = 192. A learned [cls] token is prepended, giving 17 tokens per crop.
Positional informationTwo separate learned tables: pos_embed (1, 17, 192) for patch position within a crop, and time_embed (1, 16, 192) for timestep position within the clip. Both are interpolated when the input geometry changes.
Transformer blocksPre-norm residual form, 4 blocks per stage: x ← x + DropPath(MHSA(LN x)) then x ← x + DropPath(MLP(LN x)).
Multi-head attentionh = 3 heads, d_h = d/h = 64. Per head: softmax(QKᵀ/√d_h)V; heads are concatenated and projected by W_O.
MLP / feed-forward192 → 768 → 192 with GELU. The 4× expansion ratio is fixed by DeiT-Tiny weight compatibility.
NormalisationLayerNorm in pre-norm placement (before each sub-layer), plus a final LayerNorm before the classifier.
Classification headMean-pool the 16 temporal tokens → LayerNorm → Linear(192 → 50) → softmax.
Project-specific componentsGeometry injection (box centre and scale added to each crop descriptor), reliability flag (whether the box was a real detection), and stream fusion (concatenate the three anatomical descriptors per timestep before temporal attention).

c · Novelty — borrowed, adapted, proposed

ComponentStatusBasis / what exactly is new
Patch embedding, multi-head self-attention, pre-norm MLP block, [cls] token, LayerNorm, GELUBORROWEDStandard Vision Transformer / DeiT-Tiny. Not claimed as novel.
DeiT-Tiny ImageNet initialisationBORROWEDPublic checkpoint. It is what fixes d = 192, h = 3 and patch = 16 — these are constraints, not design choices.
Factorised spatial-then-temporal attentionBORROWEDViViT factorised-encoder family.
AdamW, cosine schedule, mixup, label smoothing, weight EMA, stochastic depthBORROWEDStandard DeiT-era training recipe.
Masked-image-modelling pretrainingADAPTEDSimMIM-style objective applied to crop streams rather than full frames, and matched to the fine-tuning resolution distribution — without that match it measured as worthless (+1.9, p = 0.36); with it, +9.5.
Three anatomical crop streams instead of full framesADAPTEDStandard SLR practice is full-frame video or pose keypoints. Here a ViT operates on hand and face crops, with the streams swapped under horizontal flip so mirroring stays physically coherent.
Geometry re-injection — box centre and scale added back as a per-token featurePROPOSEDCropping deletes sign location, which is phonemically contrastive in ISL (same handshape at forehead vs chest = different words). The geometry vector restores it.
Detection provenance as a model inputPROPOSEDEach crop carries a flag saying whether its box was a real detection or interpolated from a neighbouring frame, so the model is told which inputs to distrust rather than being fed stale boxes silently.
Cache deeper than you sample (32 stored, 16 used)PROPOSEDMeasured +3.2 top-1 at zero inference cost. Also found to govern self-supervised transfer: a 16-frame pretrain on a 16-frame cache reached lower reconstruction loss and transferred 10 points worse.
Session-disjoint protocol from camera metadataPROPOSEDINCLUDE ships no signer IDs, so signer-independence is not directly constructible. Sessions are recovered by clustering the MVI_#### counter, enabling the leakage decomposition in §1.
Confidence gating as a first-class outputPROPOSEDAbstention surfaced in the UI; measured on the earlier pixel-only model, 75.6 % unconditional becomes 90.7 % on the 75 % of clips it commits to; not yet re-measured for the landmark model.
Landmarks the detector already computes, as a second inputPROPOSED21 joints per hand, made position- and scale-invariant, added to the existing crop tokens. 91 k parameters; mean 73.7 % → 86.5 % on identical clips.

07

Algorithm Procedure — Step by Step

5 marks

Mathematical, step-by-step algorithm corresponding exactly to the architecture in §6.

1 · Input

V ∈ ℝ^{F×H×W×3}, label y ∈ {1 … C} F ≈ 50-120 source frames, C = 50 classes

2 · Preprocessing — temporal sampling

eₖ = k · F / T , k = 0 … T tₖ = ⌊ eₖ + uₖ·(eₖ₊₁ − eₖ) ⌋ uₖ ~ U(0,1) training uₖ = ½ evaluation

3 · Detection and cropping

b_{t,s}, σ_{t,s} = Detect( V[tₖ] ) x_{t,s} = ( resize(V[tₖ], b_{t,s})/255 − μ ) / σ x_{t,s} ∈ ℝ^{64×64×3}, s ∈ {L, R, F} σ = provenance ∈ {direct, roi, interp, missing}

4 · Patch / token formation

x_{t,s} → { p₁ … p₁₆ }, pⱼ ∈ ℝ^{16·16·3} non-overlapping 16×16 patches, 768 dims each

5 · Embedding and positional encoding

z⁰_{t,s} = [ x_cls ; E·p₁ ; … ; E·p₁₆ ] + E_pos E ∈ ℝ^{768×192} E_pos ∈ ℝ^{17×192} learned, per patch slot

6–7 · Transformer block and attention (Stage A, ℓ = 1…4)

Q = zW_Q , K = zW_K , V = zW_V A_i = softmax( Q_i K_iᵀ / √d_h ) , d_h = 64 head_i = A_i V_i , i = 1 … 3 MHSA(z) = [ head₁ ; head₂ ; head₃ ] W_O

8–9 · MLP, normalisation and residuals

z′ = z + DropPath( MHSA( LN(z) ) ) MLP(z) = GELU( zW₁ + b₁ ) W₂ + b₂ W₁ ∈ ℝ^{192×768}, W₂ ∈ ℝ^{768×192} z = z′ + DropPath( MLP( LN(z′) ) )

Descriptor + geometry injection PROPOSED

g_{t,s} = W_g·[ cx, cy, √(w·h) ] + W_r·𝟙[ σ_{t,s} ∈ {direct, roi} ] h_{t,s} = z⁴_{t,s}[cls] + g_{t,s} ∈ ℝ^{192}

Stage B — stream fusion and temporal attention

f_t = W_f·[ h_{t,L} ; h_{t,R} ; h_{t,F} ] + E_time[t] W_f ∈ ℝ^{192×576} u = TemporalViT( f₁ … f_T ) same block form, 4 layers, over 16 tokens

10 · Classification

ū = (1/T) Σ_t u_t ŷ = softmax( W_c · LN(ū) + b_c ) W_c ∈ ℝ^{50×192}

11 · Loss

mixup over the batch λ ~ Beta(α, α), α = 0.2, applied w.p. 0.5 x̃ = λxᵢ + (1−λ)xⱼ , ỹ = λyᵢ + (1−λ)yⱼ label-smoothed cross-entropy, ε = 0.1 ℒ = − Σ_c [ (1−ε)·ỹ_c + ε/C ] · log ŷ_c floor: for C = 50, ε = 0.1 → min ℒ = 0.702 a loss resting near this value indicates memorisation rather than convergence

12 · Backpropagation

g_θ = ∂ℒ / ∂θ reverse-mode autodiff g_θ ← g_θ · min( 1, γ / ‖g_θ‖₂ ) , γ = 1.0 gradients clipped by global L2 norm

13 · Parameter update — AdamW

m ← β₁m + (1−β₁)g_θ , β₁ = 0.9 v ← β₂v + (1−β₂)g_θ² , β₂ = 0.999 m̂ = m / (1−β₁ᵗ) , v̂ = v / (1−β₂ᵗ) θ ← θ − η(s)·( m̂/(√v̂ + ϵ) + wd·θ ) η(s) = η₀·½(1 + cos( π(s−s_w)/(S−s_w) )) , s > s_w encoder LR = 0.1 × head LR; wd not applied to norms or biases θ_EMA ← β·θ_EMA + (1−β)·θ , β = 0.99

14 · Inference — TTA and ensembling

p̄ = (1 / |M||V|) Σ_{m∈M} Σ_{v∈V} softmax( f_m(x^{(v)}) ) V = 3 temporal phases × 2 flips = 6 views M = ensemble members (1 or 5)

15 · Output — confidence gate

output = argmax_c p̄_c if max_c p̄_c ≥ τ ABSTAIN otherwise τ = 0.4 chosen at the knee of the coverage curve

Read the size column with the accuracy column. The claimed headline is the last row: one model, 2.0 MB, 85.9 %, as a three-seed mean. The ensemble reaches 75.8 % but weighs 18.5 MB, and 0.2 points is one clip in 472 — inside the 2.7-point noise floor; it is promising, not established.

Comparison with the literature

Nedungadi et al. 2025[1]not stated as signer-disjoint97.5 %not stated

The TSL-ONE-S row is the only like-for-like comparison: a signer-independent protocol on a different sign language, landing at 79.7–80.8 % — the same regime as our 75.8 %.

Inference and discussion

  • +24 points came entirely from data handling — training length, frame count, cache depth and test-time averaging. The architecture never changed across that trajectory (51.7 → 59.7 → 70.1 → 75.8 %).
  • More data can be worse data. Adding 76 labelled CISLR clips (+13 % training data) cost 5.7 points, because the detector finds a left hand in 25 % of CISLR frames against 91 % in INCLUDE.
  • Lower loss is not better features. A 16-frame SSL pretrain reached a lower reconstruction loss than the 8-frame one and transferred 10 points worse — it had no temporal jitter and optimised a shortcut.
  • Training length saturates once frames increase. 250 → 2,000 epochs was worth +7.9 at 8 frames; 2,000 → 4,000 at 16 frames is +0.6, inside the noise floor. The long-training result was a symptom of the frame bottleneck, not an independent lever.
Limitations — state these before a panel asks

1. Cross-corpus transfer is at chance. Tested on a genuinely different corpus these models score ~1 %. Every number in this document is INCLUDE-to-INCLUDE. The one reassuring finding is that failure is silent: no out-of-domain clip has exceeded 0.4 confidence, so the gate degrades safely.

2. Session-disjoint is a proxy for signer-independence, not a guarantee. INCLUDE ships no signer IDs; sessions were reconstructed from a camera counter.

3. 50 words, not 262. On the full vocabulary the honest figure is 42.1 %.

4. Isolated words only. No continuous signing, no segmentation, no translation to English.

5. No evaluation on self-recorded footage. Nothing here predicts behaviour on your own camera.

The 50-word benchmark, exactly

PropertyValueVerification
Classes50all 50 have both train and test clips
Training clips57110–15 per word, mean 11.4
Test clips4726–11 per word, mean 9.4
Validation clips0folded into train — the val split shared all sessions with train and so measured nothing; final-epoch selection is used instead
Clip overlap train↔test0asserted at build time
Shared MVI session ids04 training sessions, 3 test sessions
train sessions: 3688-4112, 4197-4242, 9217-9542, 9878-9999 test sessions: 1-107, 4865-5343, 8600-8644

Vocabulary

Adjectives (loud, quiet, happy, long, short, tall, wide, narrow, big, small, slow, fast, hot, cold, warm, cool, new, old, young, good, bad, wet, dry, sick, healthy), pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they, you-plural), clothing (Hat, Dress, Shirt, T-Shirt, Pant, Shoes, Pocket), greetings (Hello, How are you, Alright, Good Morning, Good afternoon, Good evening), colours (Brown, Grey), kinship (Brother, Boy).

Preprocessing chain

Sample 32 frames uniformly across the clip → letterbox to 720×1280 → MediaPipe two-stage detection → crop three streams at 128 px → write memmap cache. At training time: sample 16 of the 32 with per-segment jitter, random-resized crop to 64 px, horizontal flip with stream swap, colour jitter, random grayscale, stream dropout, resolution jitter.

Why INCLUDE is suitable

  • Largest openly available word-level ISL corpus, recorded with experienced signers under conditions close to natural use.
  • 263 words across 15 semantic categories permits a vocabulary-size study, which turned out to matter more than any architecture change.
  • Filenames retain the camera's MVI_#### sequence counter — the only available handle for reconstructing recording sessions.

Project-specific novelty in dataset use

  1. Session-disjoint protocol from camera metadata. INCLUDE ships no signer IDs, so signer-independence is not directly constructible; sessions are recovered by clustering the counter and whole blocks held out.
  2. Leakage decomposition separating near-duplicate takes from shared sessions (§1).
  3. Vocabulary tiers ranked by total clips with a floor on held-out clips — ranking by training support instead produced a 30-word tier with only 22 test clips.
  4. A cache deeper than the model consumes (32 stored, 16 used), worth +3.2 points.
  5. A leak guard that re-reads the written split file and asserts no held-out cross-corpus clip reached training.
11

UI Screens Planned

5 marks
S1 · Home

States scope up front — 50 signs, runs offline, no server. Sets expectations before the user signs anything.

S2 · Input / capture

Detection overlay proves the camera can see the hands. Detection rate is the single best predictor of whether a prediction means anything.

S3 · Processing

Shows the pipeline stages, so a stall is attributable to a stage rather than being a mystery.

S4 · Prediction / results

Five candidates, because top-5 is 96.4 % against top-1's 85.9 %. Correcting is one tap and yields a labelled example.

S5 · Abstain

The confidence gate made visible (measured on the earlier pixel-only model, 75.6 % unconditional becomes 90.7 % on the 75 % of clips it commits to; not yet re-measured for the landmark model). It must never show a guess.

S6 · History dashboard

Every recognition with confidence and timestamp, abstentions included. Makes the system's uncertainty inspectable rather than hidden.

S7 · Sentence builder

Words accumulate into a phrase plus text-to-speech. This is assembly, not translation — the seam where a future ISL→English module would attach.

S8 · Sensitivity control

Exposes τ in the user's own words rather than as a number. The accuracy/coverage trade is theirs to set — a classroom and a hospital want different points on Figure 5.1.

Design principle running through all eight screens: never show a bare label. Every prediction arrives with its confidence, its alternatives, and a way to correct it. A 75.8 % system that admits uncertainty is more useful than a 95 % claim that cannot — and the abstain screen is what converts the honest number into a usable one.

Standard Paper

2 marks

Reference paper

“Vision transformer-powered conversational agent for real-time Indian Sign Language e-governance accessibility”

AuthorsP. Nedungadi et al.
JournalScientific Reports (Nature Portfolio)
Year2025
ArchitectureHybrid convolutional neural network + Vision Transformer, with a dynamic context–response mapping engine and a modular service layer
TaskContinuous ISL recognition, isolated words through full sentences, for e-governance services
Reported result97.5 % accuracy under optimised conditions; 6.53 s mean response time; System Usability Scale 71.83
SCImago statusverify at scimagojr.com before submission
What we do not claim. We have not reproduced their system, and their evaluation protocol is not stated in signer-disjoint terms. The comparison in §9 places our control beside their number and our session-disjoint result below it, rather than asserting a like-for-like win.

Why this is the standard reference for this application

  1. Same language, same architecture family, same deployment claim. A hybrid CNN + ViT for Indian Sign Language targeting real-time use — the closest published system to ours on all three axes, which makes it a genuine baseline rather than a loose citation.
  2. Peer-reviewed in a Nature Portfolio journal within the required window (Scientific Reports, 2025), so it satisfies the venue requirement without an exception.
  3. It sets up our contribution by contrast. They report 97.5 % under optimised conditions. We reproduce that class of number (98.5 %) with a random split and then show the same model, same words, same recipe scores 75.6 % session-disjoint. Our contribution — quantifying the protocol gap and then closing 31 points of it — is only legible against a strong published claim.
  4. It shares our end goal. Both target continuous ISL understanding for a real user, not isolated-word classification as an end in itself, so its system design is the right template for our roadmap.
